For some new projects, I've been thinking about model evaluation and model selection in meta-analysis. You can't get very far into the literature on this without running into Kullback-Leibler divergence, which is a metric for quantifying discrepancies between distributions (strictly speaking, it is not a "distance" metric because it's not symmetric). For two distributions $P$ and $Q$ with probability density functions $p(x)$ and $q(x)$, respectively, the KL divergence of Q from P is
$$
KL(P||Q) = \mathbb{E}_P\left[\log p(X) - \log q(X)\right],
$$
where $\mathbb{E}_P$ means that the expectation is taken with respect to $P$.

KL divergence is the basis of information criteria, including the Akaike, Bayesian, Deviance, Watanabe, and LOO ICs.

One of the vexing things about working with KL divergence is interpreting its magnitude. If two models differ by 4 in KL divergence, is that big and meaningful? Or trivial?
